newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain convinced labour reform pact will be radical.
newsitem.headline: Spain convinced labour reform pact will be radical.

text.p: Spain said on Sunday it was convinced a labour reform pact between unions and employers would be radical enough to ease the country's chronic unemployment.

Struggling to suppress Europe's highest jobless rate, the government is keen to secure a far-reaching accord aimed at liberalising its rigid labour market and preparing the economy for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We believe that the labour reforms that unions and employers are agreeing will be deep-seated and will modernise the Spanish economy and create jobs," Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato told journalists.
After weeks of intense talks, unions and employers reached a preliminary agreement on Wednesday that will provide the foundations for a final accord.
Employers said they were eager to clinch a final deal before Easter, but unions have warned that such an agreement could still face a number of hurdles and may not be ready until mid-April.

"We are close to an accord, but one shouldn't get over-excited as there are still a number of difficulties to overcome," Candido Mendez, Secretary General of the General Workers' union (UGT) said in an interview with Europa Press.

The government had given unions and employers until early March to reach an agreement before it stepped in and imposed its own measures. It had also threatened to legislate if the reforms were not radical enough.
On Sunday, Rato said he was confident there would be no fatal obstructions to a final accord and no need for direct government intervention.
However, some analysts and employers fear the reforms will not be profound enough to prepare Spain for EMU.
"But then there are ultra-liberal employer sectors that think an accord with unions will always be insufficient," Mendez said.
While the two sides have not expanded on the contents of the accord, they said they had reached broad agreements on permanent contracts, dismissal terms and collective bargaining.
The finishing touches to a permanent contract directed toward young workers and the long-term unemployed was proving particularly difficult to conclude, Mendez said.
"We still have not fixed the quantity for the severance pay on the new permanent contract," he said.
A key objective for employers has been to cut dismissal costs. They complain Spain's severance pay is by far the highest in the European Union and dissuades them from hiring staff.
Unions, meanwhile, are keen to see the creation of a more secure contract, especially for youths who suffer most from unemployment in Spain.
Sources involved in the negotiations said employer and union leaders would meet next Friday to discuss the draft accord.
Employer groups and unions will meet their own executive committees in the early part of the week.
